TOKYO, Japan — Recent years have seen more co-productions in anime, and there is clearly a growing curiosity about the potential for features to find extra support outside Japan.

A session at TIFFCOM on Thursday, October 29, described international co-production as “anime’s new frontier.” The panel, moderated by Masao Kawano, program manager at Into Global, included Ervin Han, co-founder and CEO of Robot Playground Media and co-director of recent Annecy winner The Violinist; Foliascope CEO Ilan Urroz; and Salamander Inc. CEO Taiki Sakurai, a producer whose screenwriting credits include Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex.

The talk was split into three distinct parts, covering the “key challenges and opportunities of international co-production,” financing models and deal structures, and going to market. Han spoke first, mentioning that TIFFCOM was where he met a co-producer as well as the composer on The Violinist. He then discussed his aims for Robot Playground, looking to find “culturally-rooted stories from Asia and introduce it to a global audience.”

Han took a moment to introduce Robot Playground’s new project, The Banquet for Hungry Ghosts, showing a trailer for one of the anthology’s stories, Egg Fried Rice. Han noted that, somewhat similarly to The Violinist, Banquet will be a “majority Asian co-production with minority European components,” with production across Singapore, Malaysia, Taiwan, and Ireland. “So the production studios are based around Southeast Asia,” Han said, “and Ireland looks after music and audio posts as a minority partner.”

After Han’s quick briefing on his ongoing projects, Urroz introduced Foliascope’s work as well as the project the company would be pitching at the Tokyo Gap Financing Market, Back to Tomioka. Urroz highlighted co-production partners in Poland, Hungary, and Belgium, as well as creatives from Japan. “That’s exactly what we want to achieve with this movie: mixing the culture, mixing the artists coming from France, from Europe, from Japan, living in a different country but sharing the same spirit; animation can be the medium to turn to any audience about feelings, about love, about friendship.”

Urroz noted that the company was already developing marketing around the film, with merchandise including a board game designed by Antoine Bauza. Foliascope has also sold the film’s subscription streaming rights to Crunchyroll, with the companies working together to release a Japanese version.

The Foliascope CEO pivoted to discussing French systems for co-production, which the panel moderator had described as “enviable” at the opening of the session. “We are super lucky in France,” Urroz said. “We have public funding for lighting, development, production, also [innovation] funds for our studio or pipeline, we have also this incredible fund for foreign production cinematography. You can be from any country in the world: if you have a co-producer in France for a little part, you can ask for money from the French system.”

“Of course, with the internationalization of production, we have also the international tax credit. It’s a tax rebate, but we have also this very very useful paper visa, talent visa,” he continued. Urroz pointed out that in America, it is much more difficult to bring in a crew from another country to work for one to three years, and said the process in France is faster. “We made the stop-motion animation feature film The Inventor with Jim Capobianco, a veteran of Disney and Pixar,” Urroz said, adding that the production used the international tax credit.

Urroz also said these funds enable studios to embrace sustainable production. “With the French system, we are capable of transforming all our studios into positive generating solar studios, all our productions are made with solar energy,” he said. “It’s an incredible fund, an incredible system, but totally open for foreign co-production.”

Urroz also pointed to Creative Europe’s MEDIA program. “We have 27 countries in the European space, but it’s open to other countries around Europe,” he said. “It’s a system that directly helps the development of new feature films, up to 60,000 euros by co-producer, and you can have up to four co-producers […] then after you can ask for an image fund that also provides some funds for distribution, for marketing, etc.”

“The very basic difference between financing in Asia and Europe is the fact that in Europe, as even a solution, you know, in some ways they are very fortunate to have a very established, structured system for financing, particularly within the EU, to the extent that a majority of the budget could be financed if it’s you know, structured the right way through soft monies, incentives, and grants, and broadcaster pre-sales,” Han said.

“In Asia, most of it is private financing. This is a fundamental difference that I’ve actually found sometimes requires quite a bit of understanding for Asia to co-produce with Europe. In Asia, there is some amount of government financing, but by and large, I think it’s maybe up to 20% at most, if you’re lucky. And the majority has to be raised privately through structured financing, through private equity, sometimes specific private equity investors, family offices.”

Asked about the pros and cons of international co-production for anime, Sakurai said he felt Japanese animation was still viewed from a narrow perspective, which complicates funding when certain expectations are tied to the term “anime.” At the same time, he has found a “high level of tolerance” when a project aligns with those expectations.

Following the other panelists’ points about government support, Sakurai highlighted that even the greatest successes are generally not made overnight. He referred to the success of Makoto Shinkai—a director he called a “genius”—who also needed many chances to break through and succeeded following 14 years of support from his producer.

Han went on to say that one real challenge for many producers in Asia is securing support from broadcasters. “It’s also why we have to go overseas. I mean, the whole idea of a [co-production] is that it’s not just finding money; it’s finding partners with complementary strengths and partners who believe in your story, in your film, in your tv series, in your project. To do it together because you cannot do it alone. You know, I think that principle is very important. Once their understanding is there, then we try to find a way.”

Just as TIFFCOM as a whole suggested a general interest in co-production, the panel showed the financial incentives driving that interest, alongside Japanese companies’ hopes of deepening their connections with global audiences. Urroz and Han’s observations highlighted a key attraction: the more extensive government support available in countries such as France compared with financing systems in Asia.

Adorable pink bears are the main attraction at Pinkooland, a theme park whose biosynthetic mascots offer visitors an encounter with something fluffy, friendly, and engineered to entertain. For the people working below ground, however, keeping that fantasy running is a considerably less appealing proposition.

With Halloween just around the corner, Cartoon Brew is debuting the trailer for director Luis Usón’s 12-minute animated short, an Ecuadorian-Spanish production that brings horror, science fiction, and corporate satire into a world built around manufactured happiness. The film recently premiered in the official short film competition at the Sitges International Fantastic Film Festival of Catalonia, and functions as a potential entry point into something far more ambitious.

Watch the trailer below:

The story follows Kassy, a park employee trapped in its underground facilities when the Pinkoos, those seemingly lovable bears, unleash chaos and destruction. It’s a premise with an immediately apparent appeal in an era of indie horror box office dominance.

“Packed with action, suspense, and ultra-violence, it’s a mind-bending journey that explores the dark and disturbing corners of ourselves and the society we live in, where pink teddy bears, ruthless corporations, and childhood dreams collide in an explosive and, above all, insanely fun experience,” Usón explains.

Produced by Ecuador’s Matte CG and Spain’s Vanova, Pinkooland brings together artists with backgrounds in animation, VFX, and video games. Usón’s experience includes layout and previs work on major studio productions, including Denis Villeneuve’s Dune. He previously co-directed the animated short Afterwork with Pinkooland producer and CG supervisor Andrés Aguilar, Ichi to his friends.

“Pinkooland is the film I’ve always dreamed of making,” Usón says. “A film for those who want to dive into a different, unexpected, and dangerous world.”

The creative team also includes animation director Cécile Brossette, whose credits include The Lorax, Despicable Me 2, and Minions, and production designer Enric Sant, who came to animation after more than a decade in video games. Usón wrote the short with María Burgués and Omar Rabuñal Varela.

For the performances, Usón worked with an actress using motion capture to develop the characters’ movements and physical interactions. That material provided a foundation that the animators refined through keyframe animation. Detailed previs and 3D layout established staging, camera movements, and timing before the team moved into final animation.

Using Unreal Engine, the filmmakers adjusted lighting, cameras, materials, and environments interactively. The team also handled hair simulation within the engine, while using Houdini for complex visual effects.

More than a standalone short, Pinkooland was also conceived as a proof of concept for a feature currently in development. Alongside introducing Kassy and the park’s unsettling universe, it gave the filmmakers an opportunity to test the production pipeline for a longer film combining horror, science fiction, and dark comedy.

For now, the trailer introduces a workplace where the cheerful branding promises far more comfort than the employees can expect.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Vinnie Ann Bose’s Sulaimani, a French production from Girelle Production and Les Astronautes. Bose’s first professional film combines stop-motion for its present-day scenes with hand-painted 2D animation for memories. It earned Oscar qualification through wins for Best Short Film at the 2025 Manchester Animation Festival and the animation jury award at the 2026 Aspen Shortsfest.

At an Indian restaurant in Paris, two women from Kerala encounter familiar flavors, sounds, and smells that stir memories of the country they left behind. Their reasons for leaving differ, as do their relationships with home. Drawing on Bose’s own experience moving to France, Sulaimani explores food as both a source of comfort and a connection to complicated histories of family, identity, and independence.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Vinnie Ann Bose: I am from Kerala, just like the two protagonists of the film. I moved to France in 2016 to study, and I started writing Sulaimani in 2018. It was a time when I was feeling very homesick. During difficult days, food from home was a big source of comfort. Sulaimani began with a simple craving for a Kerala restaurant in France.

Meanwhile, I was slowly starting to feel comfortable in France, which made me question my identity and my relationship with both countries. Sulaimani was a way for me to think through these questions and find some clarity in my life choices.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

Sulaimani is my first professional film. The production was a wonderful experience, where I learned how to direct a team, collaborate with numerous talented artists to improve the film, and experiment with techniques that I had never tried before.

But the most valuable lesson was how to find the right distance when the film’s subject is so personal. This was the biggest challenge during the script and storyboard phase, creating an emotional roller coaster until I was satisfied with the animatic. Everything that followed seemed like a walk in the park in comparison.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I wanted to use two animation techniques to distinguish the present from the past. Stop-motion feels tangible and realistic, which I felt suited the present. I believe that memories are often shaped by our emotions rather than by facts. So I felt that 2D animation, with its hand-painted images and exaggerated colors, would help retain a certain imperfection and ambiguity, just like our memories.

I wanted the characters to have subtle and natural acting, so I decided on a realistic animation style. The character design was developed accordingly, to allow subtle expressions while remaining recognizable across both animation styles.

Food plays such an important role in the film. What were the biggest challenges in bringing its textures, preparation, and sensory qualities to the screen?

It was important to me to make the food look edible and delicious, even in miniature, as it is the heart of the film. But it was very tricky to make the food look appetizing!

We used the weirdest things, like hair gel with tiny pearls to create boiling water, plastic wrap to simulate tea being poured into a glass, papier-mâché to make the porottas, and glycerin to make the chicken curry shine. It took a lot of trial and error before we reached a satisfying result.

Patrick Stewart, whose unmistakable voice brought weight to animated kings, sexually charged absurdity to some of television’s most disreputable authority figures, and dignity to a talking poop, died Wednesday, October 28, at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86.

His spokesperson said he had been living with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. His death was announced Thursday.

Known best as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, Stewart built an extensive animation career alongside his world-class performances onstage and in live action. His credits stretched from The Plague Dogs and The Prince of Egypt to The Simpsons, American Dad!, and English-language versions of films by Hayao Miyazaki and Katsuhiro Otomo.

Stewart was also an outspoken admirer of the medium. In a 2011 CNN interview, he offered an endorsement that went well beyond his own voice acting work:

I think in film the most exciting work currently is being done in animation.

Animation offered Stewart opportunities to extend the qualities audiences recognized from his famous screen characters, and, by his own account, gleefully dismantle them. He would regularly make audiences, and himself, break out into giggling fits when discussing some of his more absurd animation roles.

One of Stewart’s earliest voice acting feature credits was Major in Martin Rosen’s devastating The Plague Dogs (1982). Adapted from Richard Adams’s novel, the film belonged to a very different tradition from the family entertainment that would account for much of his later feature work.

In 1994, he voiced Adventure, the swaggering, pirate-styled book in the live-action/animated cult favorite fantasy The Pagemaster. Joining a voice cast that included Whoopi Goldberg, Frank Welker, and fellow Star Trek alum Leonard Nimoy, Stewart helped turn literary genres into physical characters.

A more imposing assignment followed when DreamWorks cast him as Pharaoh Seti in The Prince of Egypt (1998). Stewart gave the ruler the conviction of a man who considered his authority and the violence used to preserve it entirely natural. His ability to convey paternal affection alongside moral blindness lent dramatic weight to the fledgling studio’s ambitious first hand-drawn feature.

His feature career also encompassed broad comedy and science-fiction adventure. He voiced the alien King Goobot in Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius (2001), teacher Mr. Woolensworth in Disney’s Chicken Little (2005), and Max Winters in the CG feature TMNT (2007).

For English-speaking audiences, Stewart also appeared in two modern classic anime features. He played the swordsman Lord Yupa in the 2005 English-language dub of Hayao Miyazaki’s Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind and inventor Lloyd Steam in the English version of Katsuhiro Otomo’s Steamboy.

His famous Shakespearean stage career took an animated turn in 2011’s Gnomeo & Juliet, where he voiced a statue of The Bard himself.

On TV, one of his defining guest performances arrived in the 1995 Simpsons episode “Homer the Great.” As Number One, leader of the Stonecutters, Stewart presided over a secret society whose elaborate rituals disguised a collection of petty privileges and childish grievances.

Stewart’s longest-running TV animation role came when he was asked to voice CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock in American Dad! Stewart began voicing Stan Smith’s boss when the series launched in 2005, lending the character his voice and likeness for the next two decades.

Bullock turned Picard and Xavier’s authority inside out. He was reckless, vindictive, sexually uninhibited, and spectacularly unfit to wield the power he possessed. Stewart’s assured delivery made the character’s behavior even more outrageous, as did the absurdity of a senior CIA official sounding unmistakably British. Stewart joked that the writers had promised him a scene in which the other agents would finally notice his accent, a development he suggested would signal the end of the series.

Stewart spoke warmly about the role and the people behind it, describing American Dad! as a source of extraordinary professional pleasure:

It has given me as much pleasure as almost anything in my career, not just because the writing is brilliant and scabrous and offensive and provocative, but because the people themselves are such adorable people.

MacFarlane, a longtime admirer and collaborator of Stewart’s, mourned the loss of his friend on Instagram, writing:

Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us.

I grew up as a fan, and was later gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend, working with him for many years on “American Dad!”, “Family Guy”, and “Ted”. He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come. I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day 1 of a new film. He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, “Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.” We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Seth MacFarlane (@macfarlaneseth)

His most recognizable live-action characters also followed him into other forms of animation. Robot Chicken brought him back as Gurney Halleck, his character from David Lynch’s Dune, while games offered repeated returns to Picard and Professor Xavier. His Xavier performances included X-Men Legends and X-Men Legends II: Rise of Apocalypse; his Picard credits included Star Trek: Armada, Bridge Commander, and Legacy. Beyond those franchises, his game work included Emperor Uriel Septim VII in The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion and Zobek in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow.

His appetite for incongruity remained intact in The Emoji Movie (2017), where he voiced Poop. Appearing on Conan, Stewart explained that accepting the part reflected his “philosophy of finding diversity in the work that I do.”

“Thirty years ago, I probably wouldn’t have accepted this role. But I am now honored and delighted to be playing the role of the emoji poop.”

The character, he explained, would be “a very upright, very proper, rather cultivated sounding Englishman.” Stewart clearly enjoyed the absurdity of the assignment, recalling his enthusiastic response when his agent revealed the offer: “How diverse could an emoji role get? Poop is it. That’s the one.”

Born July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, Yorkshire, Stewart joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. Star Trek: The Next Generation, which premiered in 1987, made him an international star; the X-Men films brought another defining role beginning in 2000. Across those decades, animation became a recurring outlet for both his dramatic skill and his increasingly visible comic appetite.

He is survived by his wife, singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell, and his children, Daniel and Sophia.

TOKYO, Japan – Grotesqqque is a fun film title to type. An enigmatic anime feature playing at the Tokyo International Film Festival this week, Grotesqqque has a q in its name for each of the three installments that make up its omnibus structure. The film’s overarching title nods to the weird and wonderful sights in store.

The first episode in this triptych, “A(e)liens,” follows a young alien woman who crash-lands on the streets of Shibuya, where she develops a passion for Earth culture. The second, “Yoroshiku Girl,” shifts gears to an action-heavy battle royale scenario. The third, “Nocturne: Nuit Grotesque,” is the most unexpected—a slower, sapphic vampire story in a gothic apocalypse.

The project’s director, Atsushi Nishigori, is an industry veteran, celebrated for his work as character designer on the enigmatically titled cult classic series Panty & Stocking with Garterbelt and as director of the international breakout Darling in the Franxx—but he’d much rather focus on his present achievement. He directed Grotesqqque’s first and third segments himself, wrote its second, and created the original character concepts.

Animated by CloverWorks, with planning and production by JOEN and Aniplex, Grotesqqque opens in Japanese theaters on November 6. Cartoon Brew sat down with Nishigori during the Tokyo International Film Festival.

Cartoon Brew: Why Grotesqqque? It’s a word that perhaps speaks to the wild visual surrealism and “out-there” nature of this project.

Atsushi Nishigori: The film is made up of three stories—that in itself is a bit strange. It’s kind of a patchwork film, and there’s an eeriness to that.

If you make an original animation, it needs to make an impact. So, for a title that might startle or surprise an audience, Grotesqqque works very well.

Your works are defined by their anarchic visual sensibility—how did you funnel that career DNA into this project? Did you feel a simultaneous urge to push that sensibility further in the first segment and perhaps lean in a different direction in the third?

I feel that all three of the film’s segments are equally reflective of my style. They’re all things that I’ve always wanted to do but never had the chance to before. I’m an animator, a director, and a producer. Those who know me well will understand. Those who don’t might view these disparate elements as separate from each other.

Do you view Grotesqqque as being an “ultimate,” highly complete expression of your artistic identity? Does it come from your heart and feel like it belongs to you personally?

Yes, it does come from my heart. It’s a very visceral thing—that’s why I named it Grotesqqque.

How did this project first come about, and how did you pull it all together?

After I directed Darling in the Franxx, I was asked to direct a feature—but I was just too tired; I couldn’t consider it. However, I had so many visuals that I wanted to draw. If I could make a film—maybe in the mid-length region—then maybe I could do it.

Visually, there were so many styles that I wanted to pursue. I couldn’t put them together into one story. So, in the end, I decided to divide it into three and connect those pieces into one long feature—that’s how it came about.

Do you find the omnibus format to be creatively freeing? It gives you the opportunity to involve all these different styles and elements. Would you recommend that other animators pursue projects of this nature?

It’s a bit experimental; it’s a different challenge. It’s intriguing. But, at the same time, I have to be in control of the three stories at once by myself, and so I sometimes become the bottleneck of the project. It’s really difficult, so I wouldn’t recommend it to others! I understand now why the average feature is based around a single story.

Tell me about the animation process. Did it differ between the three segments?

If I made all three segments in the same style, it might have caused stress to the audience—they might get tired; they might get bored. I kept that in mind, and it was the main reason for changing up the style between the segments. I focused on action in some of them; I took longer spaces between dialogue in others.

It took fine-tuning between the different stories. I created what I wanted to create, and I created something the audience would enjoy. But to balance that all out was the biggest challenge for me.

How much of the film was drawn on paper, and how much was drawn digitally? What software did you use?

95% was drawn digitally. We mainly use Clip Studio. Some staff use the software that they themselves are used to, but it’s mostly Clip Studio.

I myself practiced hand-drawn animation up until the Rebuild of Evangelion films. After that, I switched to digital. I’m trying to keep up with the young people.

Taking a closer look at the first segment, “A(e)liens”: How do you go about designing characters? There’s an immense—and highly endearing—variety in the creatures that occupy the Shibuya that we see in this first episode.

It all draws on my past experience. I never had the intention of making something new that starts from zero. So I used the techniques and designs of my first works as a foundation—that was my aim for this project. I just drew what I wanted to draw. There was no difficulty in that.

Regarding the aliens and UFOs and little gadgets, that was some of the most fun I’ve had designing things.

It’s fascinating that this first episode tells the story of a young alien woman enjoying engaging with Japanese culture in Shibuya. It strikes me that this is very much what many foreigners do when they come to Japan and explore Tokyo—it’s that kind of interaction. And it strikes me also, of course, that this film will be enjoyed by both domestic and international audiences—which leaves me curious as to which audience you were thinking of as you created and animated this sequence.

Yes, it’s as you say. I wouldn’t know how an actual alien being would feel if she landed in Shibuya. It was much easier for me to imagine how a foreigner would feel if they came to Tokyo and interacted with Japanese culture. I wanted to depict that with comedy—with a lightness to it—so that foreigners could enjoy it.

That said, I am Japanese. If I think too much about the foreign audience from the get-go, it would end up in a different style. So I was conscious of it, yes, but my aim was to depict Japanese culture from a domestic perspective, but also for foreigners.

I love your aesthetic choices in this first segment. You go for a pastel-colored look, and that’s interesting when it’s such a recognizable Shibuya. It’s very much what we see on the street in real life, but heavily stylized in a different palette.

Well, if I depicted Tokyo as it is—too realistic—it wouldn’t be fun at all. I wanted to add a manga, comedy feel to it. But the structure and layout of Shibuya are 1:1. With the color, I wanted to add a fantasy feel. The aim was to marry the realistic with the fantasy within that frame.

Critics have noted the third segment of this film as a departure from your usual work. It’s slower, more romantic in nature—quite arthouse, almost. I’m curious about the influences that fed this segment and what led you toward this different style.

The animation that I created in the past as work—if you compare it to that, yes, it might feel different. But those who really know me might feel that it is, in fact, my style, this third section. It’s something that I’ve always wanted to do, but I hadn’t had the chance to do it. I’ve always been interested in the idea of a created family. I always had Little Women in mind. And compared to the first two, yes, it does have a calmness to it. There’s a film noir sensibility there.

Could you tell me about the film’s music? It’s an extraordinary and extensive lineup of artists that you’ve assembled—almost as kaleidoscopic and varied as the film’s visuals.

I’m no expert on music, so I enlisted the help of Sony Music—because I was able to realize this film through Aniplex. Hasegawa-san, the producer, is a music expert. I gave him my ideas of what kind of music I was aiming for, and they brought back what would match my visuals. I was hoping for chemistry to happen there, and they came back with genres that I would never have thought of myself—music that feels very current.

You’ve taken on many different roles within this project. Do you find it easy to balance them, and do some come more naturally than others? Is it useful for you to maintain overarching creative control on a project like this one?

Generally speaking, people might say that it’s not too good to have one person take on every role. But for me, it balanced out—I had the career, the experience of taking on so many roles. And I think you need that kind of experience in order to succeed when you do so. I view that as one of my strong points, and I took on this project with that in mind.

All that said, mangaka handle everything themselves. Some animators today are also doing everything by themselves. I don’t think you have to divide the work across many people. I wanted to propose that in this era, in this generation, it’s possible to take on every role by oneself.

A forbidden cornfield hides a subterranean tomb where two unsettling figures wrapped in corn husks wait in Dolores, the debut short from Mexican director Cecilia Andalón Delgadillo. Arriving online today for Halloween, the dialogue-free film draws on western Mexico’s pre-Hispanic heritage and Guadalajara’s stop-motion community to send a curious child somewhere she might never leave.

The short follows a seven-year-old girl who flees a fire demon and falls into an ancient, well-hidden grave, where two sinister inhabitants want her to stay forever. Only a kind, resourceful armadillo offers her a chance to escape. Following more than 80 festival selections and a 2025 Ariel Award nomination, the film is now available on Miyu Distribution’s Bang Bang YouTube channel.

Andalón Delgadillo began developing Dolores during the pandemic, encouraged by her husband to finally pursue a story of her own. Its ingredients were personal, drawing on family memories and her fascination with the Mexican countryside.

“Part of the inspiration comes from the stories my mother told me when I was little, about visiting a ranch in a rural area around here,” she told Cartoon Brew ahead of the short’s online release. “Part of it also has to do with one of my nieces, who was very outgoing. Somehow, the energy of Dolores’ character comes from her.”

Those elements came together around the tumbas de tiro, the pre-Hispanic shaft tombs of western Mexico. The setting also informed the armadillo character.

“I had come across something about it being a deity in the pre-Hispanic cultures here in western Mexico, connected to death,” she explained. “That seemed very interesting to me, because they’re precisely in this underground space, in the shaft tombs.”

The film’s two threatening figures connect that buried world to the cornfield above. Their designs draw on Mexican calavera imagery, with corn husks providing a material link between the two environments.

“Something very important was that they retain the corn husks,” Andalón Delgadillo said. “The corn was above them, and they preserve it in their materiality.”

Art director Mario González helped develop the characters’ appearance, while Andalón Delgadillo and Puebla-based artist Ángel Meléndez built the puppets. Her background in painting, printmaking, and theatrical puppets and masks fed into both the physical production and its staging.

“I make a lot of puppets and masks for theater, so I think that also influences some elements, even the camera direction, which is sometimes more static, as though it were theater,” she said.

That interest in working across disciplines also connects her to one of her principal influences, Jan Švankmajer.

“He doesn’t just direct or make animation. His work encompasses different disciplines: printmaking, sculpture, painting, collage,” she said. “I find that very interesting.”

Production took two and a half years, from the decision to make the film to its final master. Much of that work happened at El Taller del Chucho, where Andalón Delgadillo had worked on Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio. She first approached the studio’s director, Angélica Lares, for feedback on her screenplay before returning with a co-production proposal.

“Before El Taller del Chucho, productions were made in smaller places, in the homes and garages of the directors and filmmakers here,” she said. “Pinocchio and El Taller del Chucho mark a turning point in production models.”

Several Pinocchio crew members joined Dolores, including cinematographer Gilberto Torres. For Andalón Delgadillo, their experience helped preserve high production standards on a smaller project.

One particularly ambitious shot circles Dolores and the two skeletal figures through a complete 360-degree camera move. Animator Pablo Bedolla spent a week bringing it to life.

“That was planned from the construction of the set, from the mock-up for that shot,” she explained. “The set was made specifically for that shot. Of course, it worked for everything else, but that one was very important.”

Another challenge involved an armadillo rebuilding itself at a larger scale. Animator Nabí Orozco achieved the transformation in clay, working backward to create the effect.

“Instead of putting itself together, it was being taken apart, and then we see it in reverse in the film,” Andalón Delgadillo said. “There were several tests, and it took some time because of the particular requirements of the shot.”

“There’s a lot of magic in stop motion.”

It’s been two weeks since I left View Conference in Turin, excited about animation as an art form and exhausted by the insistence that everyone making it already uses generative AI, whether they admit it or not.

I’ve had 14 days to reflect on my experiences there, and when a press release recapping the event hit my mailbox today, it brought some of my feelings about the event into sharper focus.

There was plenty to enjoy at the annual event, which typically sees filmmakers behind the major awards-season contenders in animation and VFX descend on the northern Italian city. Interviewing Roger and James Deakins was a particular pleasure for me, an opportunity to discuss their working lives and share their enthusiasm for filmmaking with an equally enthusiastic audience. Hopefully, we can post the video, or clips from it, soon.

Our coverage throughout the week showed how much the event offered. VFX supervisor Steve Emerson unpacked the extraordinary combination of handcrafted animation and digital effects behind Wildwood. Director McKenna Harris explained why Pixar stopped Toy Story 5 production for two weeks to solve a fundamental story problem. Director Daniel Chong and producer Nicole Paradis Grindle recounted how a rejected promotional gag became Hoppers’ viral Tom the Lizard phenomenon. And Disney’s Oscar-winning producer Yvett Merino introduced us to the world of Hexed, coming out next month.

These were spirited, specific, and illuminating accounts of how films get made and find audiences.

But the AI sales pitches kept intruding, sometimes invited, other times not. The previously mentioned event recap released today declared that “Every Pixel Will Be Generated,” a conversation featuring NVIDIA’s Richard Kerris and Runway co-founder Cristóbal Valenzuela, was the “Highlight of the Week.”

That title alone presents a commercial ambition as a guaranteed future. It also didn’t jibe with conversations I had over lunches, dinners, cocktails, and coffee with some of the world’s most accomplished artists and the leaders making decisions about how their films get made.

Jeff Kember, Nvidia’s Principal Technical Evangelist for Media2 (that’s his actual job title on LinkedIn), made the argument explicit during his Creative Control in the Age of AI Agents presentation. “There’s a whole bunch of people talking about how they’re using generative AI, and then there’s also a bunch of people who aren’t talking about it, and they’re not talking about it primarily because their legal team is not letting them talk about it,” he said. “But both people on each side of this fence are both using generative AI. I don’t know anyone who isn’t.” (Shoutout to my buddy Callum at Variety who caught this quote)

Perhaps he should have attended the directors’ panel the previous evening and saved himself the embarrassment of making such a sweeping, unsupported declaration.

“We didn’t use any AI,” Forgotten Island co-director Januel Mercado said when pushed on the subject by a moderator whose question assumed both that the filmmakers had used it and that it had improved their work. Toy Story 5 co-director McKenna Harris was equally clear: “We didn’t use generative AI on Toy Story 5.”

I’ll take the filmmakers’ word on this one.

The truth is that some filmmakers will use generative AI, and others won’t. Some will experiment and abandon it. Others will find specific applications useful while rejecting the rest. Whatever you think about whether artists should use the technology, why pretend everyone will reach the same conclusion?

NVIDIA and Runway have commercial reasons to encourage adoption. Their representatives are entitled to make their case at an event like View. Artists are equally entitled to decide a tool offers them nothing they want. Telling them their choice has already been made for them is exhausting, insulting, and wrong.

The voices arguing that AI is inevitable in art also tell us not to be afraid. That people continued to paint after the camera was invented. Artists still make hand-drawn films despite the development of CG animation. If those are the comparisons they want to draw, they undermine the claims that AI will be adopted without exception, down to “every pixel.”

None of this is to say that I’m an anti-AI purist or that discussions of the technology didn’t belong at the event. Quite the opposite. It would be foolish to shove our heads in the sand and ignore a technology already having such a profound impact on the industry. But the way some speakers presented it felt disingenuous at best and deliberately misleading at worst.

Rant over.

On the whole, View was a wonderful experience, and I’m grateful I could attend. I learned a lot, met some wonderful people, and left more excited about parts of the industry than when I arrived. There was enough talent and imagination on display to suggest that the future remains considerably more open than the sales pitches would have us believe.

MeTV Toons, the television network dedicated to classic animation, will pay tribute to Eric Bauza this Saturday, October 31, with a broadcast of Hare’s to Bugs! A Bugs Bunny Celebration, followed by a selection of classic Warner Bros. shorts.

The hour-long special, which originally debuted in 2024, will air at 7 p.m. ET/PT and features Bauza discussing Bugs Bunny’s enduring appeal. For a performer whose enthusiasm for animation history was as much a part of his public presence as the voices themselves, the program offers a fitting opportunity to revisit his affection for the characters he helped carry forward.

In a statement, Neal Sabin, vice chairman of MeTV Toons parent company Weigel Broadcasting, remembered both Bauza’s artistry and his support for the network:

Eric Bauza’s undeniable talent brought new life to voices generations have loved. His talent, humor, and deep respect for the art form helped ensure that the magic of classic animation continued to resonate across generations. While his passing is an enormous loss to the animation community, the joy he brought to audiences through these beloved characters will forever continue and always remind us of him.

Eric was so supportive of our efforts with MeTV Toons as well as MeTV’s daily cartoon morning show, Toon in with Me. He went above and beyond for us, with his warmth and wit and talent to rival Mel Blanc. We mourn the loss of our dear friend.

At 8 p.m., Bugs Bunny and Friends will follow, featuring the shorts Pre-hysterical Hare, Birds Anonymous, One Froggy Evening, and Fast and Furry-ous.

MeTV Toons is available through local broadcast affiliates, major pay-TV providers, and streaming services including Philo, Frndly TV, Fubo, and DirecTV Stream. Viewers can find local availability at MeTVToons.com.

After The Violinist took the top prize at this year’s Annecy Film Festival, co-director Ervin Han is building on that momentum with A Banquet for Hungry Ghosts, an internationally co-produced anthology feature adapted from Ying Chang Compestine’s short stories.

The four stories span settings from 1930s China to 1980s Indonesia, with dishes including hot pot and beef noodles at their center. Each has its own visual identity, but all share one requirement from Han: show the food being prepared or eaten before the horror takes hold.

Singapore’s Robot Playground Media, which Han co-founded, is leading production alongside studios from Malaysia, Taiwan, and Ireland. At the Tokyo International Film Festival, Cartoon Brew caught up with Han, an executive producer on Banquet, to discuss the project.

How did you discover the book?

Ervin Han: Well, it was actually another producer friend of mine, Justin, who remains a producer on this project. [He] placed the book in front of me out of nowhere. Just the title alone – A Banquet for Hungry Ghosts – made me immediately very curious. And it’s a book of short ghost stories, and each one is based on a Chinese dish at the center of the story.

I think immediately – because we were always looking for interesting books and titles and ideas to option and adapt – what was immediately fascinating to me is the idea of animated horror with food. Particularly Chinese food! Not just because I’m Chinese, but also because we are always looking for culturally rooted ideas and stories that we could develop for a more international audience.

And the more I thought about it, the idea of Chinese food and horror just seems like a no-brainer. Because Chinese food is one of those cultural things that is immediately universal, pretty much anywhere in the world. I don’t have to explain to you what fried rice, dumplings, or chow mein are, because in every big city in the world there’s a Chinatown [laughs]. It’s where you go in the middle of the night when everywhere else is closed, right?

Is that part of why you felt that this project could work as an international co-production in this way, because everyone has their own frame of reference for the cuisine involved?

The thing about Chinese food is obviously there’s the Chinese diaspora, and every given city has its own frame of reference for what Chinese food is like. Originally, as we were developing the idea, we thought if this was set in Chinatown in Paris or in London, it would probably tackle certain kinds of thematic material and stories, compared to if it were a restaurant set in China 1000 years ago, or maybe in Singapore.

So we all bring our social or cultural context to it, but at the end of the day, it is Chinese food. There’s that universal familiarity with Chinese food, but depending on where you’re from, you also bring your own memories and feelings and preferences, experiences about how you interact with or eat Chinese food. So that to me was very interesting. At least, it gave me right away a very strong sense of the long-term potential for this as a franchise.

Of course, as we were developing, originally we had conceived it as a 10-episode series, very much along the lines of the format of Love, Death & Robots. I think it was quite clear a couple of years in that the market for original series was extremely challenging.

We were in production on The Violinist at the time, our first feature film, and I had a bit of a better sense of how a feature project could come together. And I suspected that if I could package this as a feature, the route to financing and a potential green light… it would still be difficult, but I could still see a way because I feel there’s more room for original stories in independent features, and that was the route we took. And it happened much quicker. Within a year or so, I was able to pull together a few co-producers and even got Toonz Media Group on board to handle international sales.

Also, I wanted to set it actually more in Southeast Asia for this feature, these four stories. To me, it was a very interesting and exciting chance to bring together some pretty terrific animation talent from across Southeast Asia.

How is the work divided among the studios?

The main animation studios are actually from Singapore, Malaysia, and Taiwan. In Singapore, we are tackling two episodes. In fact, “Egg-Fried Rice” we actually completed much earlier, because that was initially commissioned as a pilot by Mediacorp, the Singaporean broadcaster.

So we are tackling one more episode, and the episodes that we’re doing are all traditional 2D. Another episode is by a Malaysian studio called Studio Climb. They’re based in Kuala Lumpur. Spencer Ooi, who is the founder of Studio Climb, also serves as overall creative director for the film across the four stories. And then we also work with Xanthus Animation out of Taipei in Taiwan. They will handle one episode. So Malaysia and Taiwan have one episode each.

And then in Ireland, we work with Telegael, our co-producer. Telegael is a subsidiary of Toonz Media Group, so they’re handling all music and audio post [production] for all four stories. So we have two Irish composers on this project, which is very interesting.

How did you choose the four stories?

We actually only picked two from the book. The other two, we created. They are actually original, so they’re based on the concept that the book has laid out, but they are original stories. The reason being, I thought that with the first feature, this first iteration of this IP out of the gate, I wanted a specific tone and a couple of dishes that are more familiar. Because the book itself, actually, if you look at the book, many of the dishes are quite specific to Chinese culture. They might be even a little bit too esoteric for a mass audience.

Of course, egg-fried rice, that’s quite well known. I wanted hot pot in there, and I think I wrote the initial treatment for “Hotpot” myself because it is something that is not uniquely Chinese. Even though mala hot pot from Chongqing, China, has become quite iconic in the culinary landscape, many cultures have a version of hot pot: a pot, a bowl, or a big bowl of broth that you cook raw food in.

“Tang Yuan” is a bit more specific. They are basically glutinous rice balls, cooked in a lightly sweet kind of a syrup; a very simple but very symbolic Chinese dish. It’s something that symbolizes reunion and togetherness. We eat a lot of that during the winter solstice, during weddings and birthdays. We developed a really cool, folkloric ghost story around it.

How did you approach each story’s visual style?

We gave a lot of the studios, even our own team, a pretty long leash. Each of these episodes has [its own] director, right? And I wanted each story to have a distinct voice and identity, tonally as well as visually. So I did not prescribe any specific style or references. We started with the stories. We discussed the stories among the group, and it’s for the director and their own team to really explore the visual side from the very beginning. And then we go back and forth.

Each of the four stories has a different visual style. I wouldn’t say they are drastically different because we pretty much split two episodes. But still, there are quite noticeable and distinct qualities that the respective art teams really brought to the project. That was very evident from the first few rounds of visual development that came back.

With the Taiwan team’s “Tang Yuan,” because it happens during the winter solstice, there’s a very bitter coldness to the palette. It’s set in a fishing village, I think in the 1950s in one of the Taiwanese provinces. It feels very folkloric, like a very traditional and quiet ghost story. (And the central ghost is a water ghost.)

Then “Hotpot,” done by the Malaysian studio [Climb]. It’s red, it’s loud, because it’s more satirical, a dark comedy, really. And there are creatures involved, so it’s got much more of a carnivalesque vibe to it. Very fun and very appetizing, in a way.

“Beef Noodles” is a dark, historical, political kind of horror. So it’s much more bleak, but it’s got a very, very heart-wrenching father-son story at the center of it. It’s set in Indonesia during the 1980s.

And then “Egg-Fried Rice,” the very first one we did, has a more opulent but also feudalistic [tone]. It’s in China, again during winter, in the 1930s. I remember with that one, we specifically referenced a couple of films from Zhang Yimou, the Chinese director, particularly Raise the Red Lantern. Very feudalistic, but also claustrophobic. Even though the settings are large and quite expensive, there’s something suffocating about it.

And it is the ideal way to explore these different tones around Asia. It goes back to your earlier question. That was the potential that I saw very early on. We couldn’t really do this with just any other anthology or something from comic books or whatever. But because it is based on food, Chinese food, I think it really lends itself to exploration of all these different creative directions.

What makes animated food look good?

Well, thank goodness I’m not animating it. [Laughs.] But I think it’s what makes animation interesting to me in the first place, that you are drawing things and making them come alive in a way that’s not real.

I mean, to quote that famous phrase, it’s the illusion of life. We are trying to create life out of something, just drawings. And I think food needs to appeal to more than just our sense of sight.

So it’s not about making it look realistic; it’s about making it look alive. And I think one of the things I did mandate to each team is that in every episode we have to see food being prepared or being eaten.

I mean, this is what the likes of [Studio] Ghibli do best, right? Taking your time to animate food being made, being prepared, being cooked, and being eaten.

The bigger challenge is, at some point in time, this food is gonna turn into something or start to open up into something quite horrifying.

Just a few weeks ago, I was looking at some of the dailies from “Beef Noodles.” It’s an oily red broth that the beef is cooked in, and yes, it’s suggestive of blood, but at the same time, it looks delicious! In an animated way, I mean. That’s very exciting, and that’s what the team is having fun exploring. I mean, under tremendous time pressure, but also having fun.

How far along is production?

We only began production proper at the start of this year. “Egg-Fried Rice” was completed much earlier because of the pilot commissioned a couple of years ago. Even though we had only finished about 80%, we have finished it since.

The other episodes really only began this year, and our current target is to finish it by April [2027]. So it’s just under a year and a half. Seems like a short time, but it’s really multiple tracks at the same time. So about a year and a half to finish a short film. Not a lot of time, but at the same time it’s what we feel is realistic, given a budget. Hopefully by April next year, just in time for the festival season.

What are you working on next?

I’m trying to find time to work on my script for what hopefully would be my next film. I have a first draft. I’m going through a second pass.

It’s a fantasy adventure, so it’s very different from what I’ve been involved in these few years, including Banquet. It’s more of a family film, but it’s based on a play written by my father 40 years ago – my dad’s a playwright.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Connie Qin He’s Dear Upstairs Neighbors, produced by Márcia Mayer. The film combines artist-created storyboards, designs, and 2D and 3D animation with generative AI models fine-tuned on the team’s concept art to create its final painterly imagery. It qualified for Oscar consideration by completing a one-week theatrical run.

Desperate for sleep, Ada finds herself increasingly consumed by the noise from the apartment above her. As she imagines what her neighbors could possibly be doing, everyday frustration gives way to elaborate, surreal fantasies. Inspired by He’s experiences during the pandemic, the film’s shifting textures, colors, and visual styles follow its protagonist’s escalating emotions.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Connie Qin He: The story came directly from my experience living in an apartment building during the pandemic. Like a lot of people, I was suddenly spending almost all my time at home, hearing all kinds of strange noises from upstairs and imagining what on earth my neighbors were doing that could be so loud.

Eventually, I decided to channel that frustration into something creative, and the moment I started putting those emotions into storyboards, I felt relieved. I’ve always loved visual storytelling, and animation felt like the perfect way to turn such a relatable experience into something surreal, funny, and emotionally expressive.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

One of the biggest lessons was the magic that happens when artists and researchers work hand in hand. We were trying to create something that hadn’t really been done before, combining a very specific painterly visual style with animation, and there was no playbook to follow.

We had to build both the visual approach and production pipeline from scratch, figuring things out one step at a time. The most successful moments came directly from that close collaboration, with artists bringing creative goals and researchers helping develop the tools and workflows to support them.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I grew up in a family that loved art. My father is an abstract fine art painter, and I spent a lot of time in galleries and museums, fascinated by how artists could express emotion through color, texture, and different materials. I’ve always wondered how we could bring that kind of artistic expression into animation.

With Dear Upstairs Neighbors, we wanted the visual style to reflect Ada’s emotional journey, becoming increasingly surreal and expressive as her frustration builds. Combining 2D and 3D animation with painterly aesthetics gave us the freedom to bring her feelings to life in a really unique way.

What surprised you most about working with AI on the film, creatively or otherwise? And is it something you will continue to integrate into your workflow?

What surprised me most was how the models could learn from and interpret the artwork our artists created. We initially hoped they would pick up on things like brushwork and color palettes, but they also began recognizing more subtle visual choices, like two-point perspective and the way we used brushstrokes to represent sound. That opened up some really exciting creative possibilities.

I’m always interested in tools that help artists tell stories in new ways, and this experience showed me how AI can support very specific creative goals. Ultimately, technology should always serve the story and the artists behind it.

Kristina Dufková’s Living Large and Marta Reis Andrade’s Dog Alone won the top feature and short film prizes, respectively, at the fifth Emile Awards. Celebrating the year’s top European animation achievements, the 2026 ceremony took place on October 28 in Krakow, Poland, during the 33rd Etiuda&Anima International Film Festival.

It’s safe to say this year’s feature winner was a real shock, given the category’s competitive field. The Czech-Slovak-French co-production beat out the Oscar-nominated, Annecy Cristal-winning Arco; the Oscar-nominated, Annecy Audience Award-winning Little Amélie; former Oscar-nominated director Claude Barras’s latest, Savages; and the latest from legendary French director Jean-François Laguionie, A Boat in the Garden. That’s some pretty heady company.

Living Large tells the story of Ben, a music-loving 12-year-old whose confidence is shaken by bullying about his weight. Adapted from Mikaël Ollivier’s novel, the film combines stop-motion puppets with hand-drawn passages that explore its protagonist’s inner life. As Dufková explained in our interview, she discovered the book while reading with her daughter and saw an opportunity to address an age group too rarely served by animated features. The film previously won Annecy’s Contrechamp Jury Award.

Dog Alone, produced by Portugal’s BAP Animation Studio and France’s Ikki Films, adds its Emile to a run that includes the Quirino Award for best short. Drawing on Andrade’s own experiences, it connects the loneliness of an abandoned dog, her widowed grandfather, and a young woman returning from London. Recorded family voices anchor translucent drawings and painted imagery, continuing BAP’s distinctive exploration of the space between documentary and poetic invention.

Ugo Bienvenu’s Arco was the evening’s only multiple winner, taking the feature prizes for backgrounds, character design, and soundtrack. Other winners included Savages for feature animation and On Weary Wings Go By for experimental short.

Saturday Morning Cartoons United has postponed The Heroes of Townsville, its Powerpuff Girls reunion fundraiser scheduled for November 7 at Glendale’s Alex Theatre, after co-founder Eric Bauza’s sudden death. Organizers said there are no plans to reschedule at this time.

Bauza, who was set to host the evening, died October 25 at age 46. The previously announced event was to bring together series creator Craig McCracken, artists Lauren Faust and Paul Rudish, and original voice cast members Catherine Cavadini, Tara Strong, and E.G. Daily, with Linda Simensky moderating.

“The outpouring of love from fans and the animation, film, and voice-over communities has meant so much to us,” the organization wrote in its announcement.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Saturday Morning Cartoons United™ (@cartoonsunited)

VIP Package ticket holders can request a full refund by emailing info@cartoonsunited.com. General admission ticket holders should contact the Alex Theatre directly for refunds.

Those who prefer to donate the cost of their ticket to Bauza’s family can do so by not requesting a refund, organizers said.

We have a strict rule here about not linking to individual GoFundMe, Kickstarter, Patreon, or similar fundraising pages. That said, anyone visiting the Saturday Morning Cartoons United website may happen to find a Patreon link at the bottom of the page, with proceeds going to Bauza’s family.

The team, led by Bauza’s fiancé, Caro Beurmann, asked for patience as it responds to inquiries while grieving its co-founder. “Please know that every inquiry will be addressed and every ticket holder will be taken care of,” the statement said.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Jocelyn Charles’ God Is Shy (Dieu est timide), produced by Remembers in France. The cosmic horror short contrasts saturated colors and cartoonish characters with increasingly disturbing imagery. Its festival run has yielded at least seven Oscar-qualifying awards, including wins at Annecy, Bucheon, Interfilm Berlin, and the Hong Kong International Film Festival.

During a train journey, Ariel and Paul amuse themselves by drawing their greatest fears. Their game takes a darker turn when Gilda, a mysterious fellow passenger, joins the conversation with a very different understanding of fear. Drawing on his fascination with metaphysical questions and the supernatural, Charles moves from a familiar social encounter toward the unsettling possibility of a universe beyond human comprehension.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Jocelyn Charles: First of all, I found horror to be a very fertile genre to explore through animation. I felt there were so many images and graphic situations I could play with. I had already experimented with horror in two music videos, and I felt that with a more complex story, I could take it much further.

I’m also fascinated by metaphysical questions and the supernatural. In the spirit of Lovecraft, I wanted to play with the immensity of the universe, an immensity so vast and unreasonable that it becomes almost unreal, and therefore terrifying. I later discovered that this was called cosmic horror, and that it was a genre in its own right, somewhere between science fiction and horror.

I think I may continue exploring subjects in that direction.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

I learned an enormous amount while making this film. One of the main things was the importance of a character’s personality, and how much their individual traits can influence the story.

I think there is a tendency in animation to create characters that are either caricatural or somewhat flat. I wanted to create characters who, thanks in large part to the voice actors, could become unique, believable, and subtle. I really understood the importance of that during the voice recording sessions.

I also learned how important it is to have a production designer whose mind is completely focused on the set design, on putting together the furniture, the objects, and all the little details that make a world feel believable and alive.

And, above all, I discovered what kind of films I like making. I like taking the codes of live-action filmmaking as a starting point rather than trying to make a purely visual film. I want to take advantage of what animation can do to transcend certain emotions or certain scenes, and push them somewhere further than live action necessarily could.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I spent a long time hesitating between two approaches. One was to have the characters and the environments treated in the same way, in order to create a strong overall graphic coherence. The other was to make the backgrounds much more painterly, while keeping the characters much flatter, closer to the look of a more traditional cartoon.

In the end, I chose the second option. I wanted the backgrounds to have a felt-tip, hand-drawn quality, because I felt that the charm of traditional techniques could make the film more visually enjoyable than having everything follow the same graphic treatment, with flat areas of color like the characters.

I also wanted the colors to be saturated, so that the film would feel fun and visually pleasing, almost playful or even comical at times. For the same reason, I gave the characters slightly cartoonish proportions, with large heads. This allows us to focus more on their eyes and mouths rather than on their entire bodies.

All of these choices were also intended to create a contrast with the horrific nature of the story. I wanted the film to be visually inviting and playful while dealing with something much darker underneath.

Why did you choose fear as the idea around which to build the film, and what interested you about exploring it through these three characters?

I think horror has often been treated as a kind of subgenre, almost as if it were something inherently cheesy or disposable. But over the past few years, with filmmakers like Jordan Peele, Ari Aster, or Julia Ducournau, horror has gained a different kind of recognition, and I was eager to explore what the genre could bring to animation.

Because, ultimately, animation can deal with any kind of story. It can be a crime film, a comedy, film noir, fantasy, science fiction, and so on. But horror allows you to add another color to that spectrum, another dimension of emotion.

And I think that is one of the strengths of animation: being able to play with that additional dimension and explore fear in a way that can be both visually striking and emotionally powerful.

BUSAN, South Korea – The animation art of Rintaro is both singular and incredibly long-lived. The programming at the 31st Busan International Film Festival, held October 6–15, offered a reminder of that. The festival’s special focus program on Japanese animation featured Japan’s first feature-length color animated film, the 1958 Toei Animation film The White Snake Enchantress, on which Rintaro has a credit as an in-between animator.

The director also worked with the likes of Osamu Tezuka during the founding of Mushi Production, specifically as an episode director on series like Kimba the White Lion and the 1963 Astro Boy, the latter also a major milestone in the history of anime. Not that Rintaro’s legacy is defined by the work of others: his work as director of the Leiji Matsumoto adaptations Galaxy Express 999 and its sequel Adieu Galaxy Express 999, through to works like The Dagger of Kamui and, more recently, Metropolis, is remarkable and one of a kind in its own right.

Visiting the festival for a masterclass, Rintaro spoke to Cartoon Brew at a roundtable interview shared with a journalist from Korea’s Cine21, reflecting on the changes to the industry he has witnessed over his illustrious career.

Following mention of his masterclass, titled A Living Legend in Japanese Animation, the now-85-year-old director was asked about what he considered turning points in Japanese animation, and whether he knowingly set out to steer the course of the industry, still in its infancy when he began working.

“I just try to create something new, something that has not existed before. And back then I didn’t really have a lot of film or video works available, so it was easy for me to find something new or create something new,” he says. “But these days, from the moment you wake up, the moment you go to bed, you are surrounded by content. So it’s difficult to find something new, or create something new [today].”

Speaking more about what set his work apart, Rintaro described his work – when pushing for more cinematic animation in the Japanese industry – as taking the form of a sort of collage.

“When it comes to Disney animation, you have a very natural style; how it differs from my work is that I use montage, so I overlap these montage images to create animation,” he says. “So, for example, if you watch this particular part of a big picture, we get closer to that part, and that’s called montage. And the same device or tool is used in Galaxy Express 999, and that’s why my works are different from general works of animation. In Japanese animation, we have a central axis or frame that you follow naturally to create a work of animation, but my work departed from that framework. The same has been done by other Japanese animators like Osamu Tezuka, and we have been at the forefront of this new type of animation.”

When it comes to learning from the past, Rintaro has kept this mindset through to his most recent works, such as the short film Nezumikozo Jirokichi, a tribute to pioneering Japanese filmmaker Sadao Yamanaka that imagines what one of his lost films might have looked like. Asked about embracing an older cinematic language in the present day, Rintaro responded that the imagery of silent film persists.

“When I studied film, you learn that the origin of film lies in silent film, and the images created by silent film filmmakers are actually very much still in use these days,” he says. “They’re very valid to this day. So out of respect for silent films, I decided to create this film. So people in contemporary society go back to silent films if they’re interested, but they don’t really think of silent film as the origin of all films. But silent films carry the soul, or the essence of film,” he says.

Besides looking at the past, both his own career and film history in general, Rintaro was also looking forward. A few of his answers suggested unease about the overstimulation of modern engagement with art, which became a common theme of the roundtable. The conversation continued into the filmmaker’s perspective on how viewership has been transformed by streaming, particularly the binge-watching encouraged by full-season drops rather than weekly releases.

“From the viewpoint of a fan, it’s wonderful that you get to watch everything without having to wait for the next installment,” Rintaro considers. “But in the entire landscape of film and cinematic culture, I think you can actually take a certain sense of joy or pleasure from this experience of waiting for the next installment that many people these days don’t experience.”

The idea of “content” perhaps hung over the rest of the conversation as it turned toward the current culture of remaking popular works. Asked about this trend and what it means for originality in animation, Rintaro responded: “I think this focus on the market worldwide has been the cause because it brings more money in to bring things back from the past that are already safe and popular.”

He continues, “But this and what we artists or writers pursue, there must be a balance between the two. So that’s why when people bring back works from the past – and I don’t think that’s necessarily a bad thing – that doesn’t contribute to creating a new future. So if we were to create a new future, then we have to embrace the risks involved, and on different social levels, try to resist current trends as well. Because at this rate, there will be no future.”

The director then linked the culture of animated remakes to the ongoing issue of generative AI.

“If we look at society from above, AI will also be pushing towards remaking works from the past because AI is about recommending the mean or the average, and that is the safe option that you can recommend. So it will not actually recommend for you to create something with risks or something more original, or there will be a situation where original ideas, original works, will not be as successful as before,” he says. “The conversation or the discussion around the originality or the creativity of AI will continue into the future. So this is a task that we must all look into and face together. As a global community, I think we have a huge burden or a task on our backs, on our shoulders.”

The Cine21 reporter went on to ask Rintaro about collaboration with AI, contextualizing the question by mentioning the wave of people using generative AI to make “Ghibli-style” images. Rintaro responded that, in terms of the impact on animation, “whether or not they use AI tools is up to the producer of each project,” going on to say that “so, as a director, I do think about how to use AI, but I would want to do it very, very carefully.”

When asked for their own opinion, the Cine21 reporter spoke about being skeptical of AI because it can only use what is borrowed.

Rintaro responded with a couple of takes, each perhaps a little more skeptical than the last. First, he likened AI to a blade, with its own uses but a high likelihood of danger if mishandled. He then added that “one year, I came across a scary story about a mother who actually studied on her tablet how to draw pictures of her child to bring different Lego blocks on the screen to complete the picture and color it in as well.”

He continues, “Now what’s really scary is that AI has the entire recipe, telling her exactly what to do every step of the way, and instead of her selecting what colors she wanted to use, she was told which color to use for each part. After she completed the picture, she congratulated herself.”

He adds, “And it just goes to show we have lost the ability to think sometimes, and we do exactly as we are instructed. And I think that’s very symbolic of what’s happening to us, and how far AI has kind of made its way into our everyday lives – and we need to think about how far we’ve let AI into our everyday lives.”
